Customer: Datadog's main advantage is correlating data across APM, custom metrics and logs via tagging, densely linked across the platform, plus built-in notebooks. Had to use OTel for Elixir apps since there's no DD SDK for Elixir/Erlang. On-demand pricing gets expensive fast, but replicating it self-hosted would require hiring another engineer.
"DataDog Don't Discount": compared to most enterprise vendors it's much harder to get a discount from Datadog; most vendors give ~1/3 off for committing to spend, Datadog doesn't.
Another user says they've never been able to negotiate Datadog down in years; price is always what's on the website, which they don't mind compared to bazaar-style vendor haggling.
Counterpoint: spending a few thousand a month, their account manager adjusts the monthly commit quarterly, giving roughly a 20% discount off website prices.
User at a medium-sized unicorn complains Datadog doesn't default to UTC or clearly label time zones on logs/graphs, causing confusion during prod outages about whether timestamps are PST, CST or UTC.

Notebooks are used for incidents (metrics side by side with comments), long-term reliability debugging, and performance tuning; widgets can be moved between dashboards and notebooks, and state lives in the URL so views are easy to share in Slack.
Critic: Datadog's data correlation is awful compared to Honeycomb, Dynatrace and Instana; users end up sifting through outdated dashboards and notebooks instead of being shown anomalies.

Company spending over $6M/yr left Datadog for Grafana despite leadership being DD fans. DD was easier for everyone, had useful baked-in features (apdex) and let non-devs build dashboards, but they left over lack of billing transparency and an incompetent account rep who angered finance and embarrassed the CTO.
User: Datadog solves a real and burning problem for product engineering teams, and though expensive, is worth every penny.
Long-time customer: the product has always been amazing, absolutely reliable and beautifully designed; they never once flinched at the bill.
Negative experience: difficult setup and tracking, with trace collection much more resource-intensive than New Relic; support emails went unanswered until a coworker complained publicly on Twitter.
Used Datadog and New Relic in large-scale production apps and, for the cost, still not very impressed by the developer experience/UX.
Favourite Datadog features: clicking a field to make it a custom search dimension in one more click, and flame graphs.
Datadog is cool but the price is ridiculously high for small orgs.
Contrasting view: Datadog is one of their favorite providers; pricing is great for small businesses but probably unaffordable for larger ones.
Datadog's server hexagon map chart praised as an innovative, standout visualization.
User wants a local-development "Datadog Lite". Datadog has no local option for verifying tracing and metrics before shipping, and Grafana is too bloated and poorly documented for that use case.
Harsh UI critique: the Datadog interface felt like a product where no one in the org ever said no to an idea, "very Atlassian."

Likes Datadog but finds it prohibitively expensive for monitoring serverless AWS apps, even with negotiated rates; the Datadog bill is many orders of magnitude higher than their AWS bill, so they're looking for alternatives.
Outlier analysis cited as a key advantage of Datadog and New Relic over open-source alternatives.
Datadog is stupidly expensive for what it provides. Don't recommend and I hope something open kills it soon.
Commenter says Datadog's APM traces are the one thing that locks companies into Datadog, and that being able to export that data would make it much easier to move to something else.

We switched to the OpenTelemetry agent from the Datadog agent. Of the commercial providers tried (Honeycomb, New Relic, Lightstep), Datadog was the worst at showing traces properly. It captures mostly the same traces, but they all show io.opentelemetry.something in the UI, making them very hard to read.
Datadog support is hot garbage. For the amount of money I've sent them over the years, they ignore feature requests and just DGAF about customers. They're very hot on licensing though.
Hoping this leads to Datadog launching a logging solution that does not cost an arm and a leg at scale.

I hate Datadog; we use their name as an epithet for how not to sell or market. Their selling tactics circa 2015-2018 completely burned us out: endless calls and emails. An AWS re:Invent Lambda talk turned out to be a thin rehash pitched by a Datadog employee.

Execs and managers seem to love DD and get upsold all the time, then ask engineers to implement half-baked features. It seems good for alerts and dashboards for infrastructure teams. But for an engineer, using it for log analysis is more annoying than tracking down the relevant logs and grepping.
I used it in my previous job and loved it. I love how quick they were to add support for new things and how easy it was to configure everything.
Love the product through and through. My only annoyance is that 'live tail' and log lines in general show up from the top scrolling down, the opposite of how regular logs scroll.

Love their product, hate their shady billing. Custom Metrics usage wasn't billed for a long time. Then they soft-launched billing without notice and my bill jumped almost 400%. I've been trying to get a refund for over 20 days through endless escalations up to C-level.
Their sales teams are ridiculously aggressive. I've received 9+ calls from them this month after telling them my org isn't interested. It's soured me on them altogether.
Sales/marketing too aggressive: they cold-called my private number despite the do-not-call list. At conferences their booth staff kept walking alongside me pitching after I said 'not interested'.
My service contract expired and I opted not to renew because the synthetics product's price rose 100x from its initial release. The product is reliable, but billing is troubling.
I've used both Datadog and New Relic in large-scale production apps, and for the costs I'm still not very impressed by the DX/UX.
My two favourite Datadog features: 1) clicking on a field and making it a custom search dimension in another click, and 2) flame graphs. Delicious flame graphs.
Datadog's one of my favorite providers, and their pricing is great for small businesses, but probably unaffordable for larger businesses.
Datadog's server hexagon map/chart thingie is something else. The kind of innovation that wins prizes.

I like DataDog, but it is prohibitively expensive for monitoring serverless applications, even with negotiated rates. Paying for DataDog is many orders of magnitude higher than our AWS bill; we're looking for alternatives.
We just moved away from Datadog because their log storage pricing is too high for us. We moved to BigQuery instead, but the interface kind of sucks.
